source: Zhang, Lin, Wu, Sun, Li, Li, Peng (2026) Useful Memories Become Faulty When Continuously Updated by LLMs
finding: Gap 6: the paper is real and was re-opened (arXiv 2605.12978, v2 29 Aug 2026). Memory built by LLM rewriting of trajectories first helps, then degrades, and can fall below no-memory. It is not only ARC-AGI: it also shows on ScienceWorld, WebShop, ALFWorld and AppWorld.
numbers: ScienceWorld score peaks near step 20 and declines through step 100 (batches of 4). WebShop: AWM goes 0.64 at 8 examples to 0.20 at 128 examples, equal to no-memory 0.20. ARC-AGI, GPT-5.4: no-memory pass@1 58.5 +/- 5.4 (10 runs, 33 tasks), consolidated epoch 1 55.1 +/- 4.9, epoch 10 38.5 +/- 5.3; pass@10 coverage 100% (33/33) to 66.7% (22/33) to 60.6% (20/33). The headline 54% is a 19-problem slice solved at 100% without memory.
quote: memory utility first rises, then degrades, and can fall below the no-memory baseline
limits: The authors build the ARC-AGI Stream testbed themselves; consolidators are their own re-implementations of ACE, AWM, DC plus a generic rewrite loop. Mostly GPT-5.4 and Qwen3.5. Self-reported, single group; no independent replication found (search quota was out).
agent_relevance: A schema that rewrites stored cases into lessons after every task risks losing solved-task coverage. Keep raw cases; make rewriting rare and gated.

source: Zhang et al. (2026) Table 4: episodic-only (raw trajectory) control vs consolidators on AppWorld and ALFWorld
finding: Appending raw trajectories to context is competitive with or better than lesson-style consolidators (ACE, AWM, Dynamic Cheatsheet) in most rows. This extends the consolidation harm beyond ARC-AGI.
numbers: ALFWorld task success (no memory / all raw trajectories / 16 raw trajectories): GPT-5.4-Mini 54 / 90 / 77; GPT-5-Mini 52 / 81 / 67; Claude-Haiku-4.5 79 / 92 / 73. AppWorld TGC (no memory / all raw): Qwen3.5-27B 66 / 73; GPT-5-Mini 14 / 23; Claude-Haiku-4.5 68 / 66 (no gain). Red marks in the table show consolidators beaten by at least one raw-log baseline in the same row. Only the first columns are cited because PDF text extraction of the rest of the table is garbled.
limits: Raw logs in context grow without bound, so the raw baseline is not equal-token against compact lessons.
agent_relevance: Strong evidence for keeping raw cases as the default store. A compact lesson store only wins when token budget forces it.

source: Zhang et al. (2026) Table 5: stripping parts of the streamed update
finding: In-place rewriting is the most damaging step. Moving toward append-only raw episodes improves accuracy step by step. Pruning (delete) without rewriting is fine.
numbers: ARC-AGI Stream, GPT-5.4, batch size 1, step 400: default in-place rewrite 43.2; append-only with prior store visible 50.0 (+6.8); add plus delete without in-place edit 64.0 (+20.8); append-only with prior store hidden 70.0 (+26.8); raw trajectories with no consolidation 76.6.
limits: One synthetic task family; one backbone for this table.
agent_relevance: Deletion by itself is not the problem; overwriting is. Our S9 should add and prune cases, never edit a stored case in place.

source: Zhang et al. (2026) Table 3 and Auto-mode ablation (agent chooses Retain, Delete, Consolidate)
finding: Stream decay on a 400-step stream: frontier coding agents that manage their own memory rise above no-memory, peak, then fall back. When the agent may choose, it keeps raw episodes by default and abstracts sparingly. Episodic management only (retain and delete, no abstraction) matches or beats full Auto.
numbers: ARC-AGI Stream accuracy (no memory / peak / step 400): GPT-5.5 78.0 / 80.0 / 68.0; Claude Sonnet 5 40.0 / 58.0 / 48.0; GLM 5.2 22.0 / 44.0 / 22.0; DeepSeek V4 Pro 28.0 / 40.0 / 18.0. Removing the episodic store and keeping only abstract lessons collapses accuracy back to the no-memory baseline. The abstract says Auto doubles the accuracy of forced consolidation.
limits: 400 steps is shorter than the over-1000-task stream in gap 4. Tasks come from one generator family, so shift is not tested. Decay here is driven by consolidation, not by a success-only bank.
agent_relevance: Evidence for retain and delete over consolidate as the default S9 action set. Does not test long-stream decay of a plain success-only bank.

source: Zhang et al. (2026) mechanism analysis: batch heterogeneity and over-general lessons
finding: Three separable failure causes: compression error, conditioning on prior memory, destructive rewriting. Mixed-task batches erode memory faster than single-task batches. Over-general lessons mislead on near tasks (a Pick&Place lesson applied to Pick-Clean-Place in ALFWorld).
numbers: Memory surgery: removing one WebShop workflow (W8) that caused click[Next >] dead loops raises pass rate. Consolidating the same trajectories in one pass beats streaming them.
limits: Mechanisms are inferred from case studies, not large controlled counts.
agent_relevance: If we distill lessons at all, do it per task family and keep the source cases linked so a bad lesson can be checked and removed.

source: Guo et al. (2026) CASCADE arXiv 2605.06702: per-task spread and what 20.9% could be
finding: Gap 9 partly closed. The abstract says 20.9% macro-averaged success over zero-shot on 16 tasks, but the text never says whether it is relative or absolute. On the 12 single-turn tasks with Qwen3-32B the absolute gain is 18.35 points (66.68 vs 48.33; 38% relative), and the per-task spread is wide: 2.1 to 51.2 points.
numbers: Qwen3-32B zero-shot to CASCADE per task (points): DDXPlus 63.77 to 84.54 (+20.8); MIMIC-IV-MR 12.79 to 63.98 (+51.2); MIMIC-IV-MSR 51.36 to 56.79 (+5.4); MIMIC-IV-TLP 48.56 to 52.25 (+3.7); MUD 25.53 to 62.44 (+36.9); CMDL 39.12 to 60.26 (+21.1); Banking77 66.66 to 84.66 (+18.0); SEntFiN 34.30 to 47.72 (+13.4); RCA 45.36 to 70.76 (+25.4); LFD 84.05 to 86.15 (+2.1); SPIDER 63.84 to 75.41 (+11.6); BIRD 44.65 to 55.18 (+10.5). Median +15.7; mean +18.35. Four of 12 tasks gain under 6 points. Zero-shot averages by backbone: Qwen3-4B 43.88, Qwen3-8B 43.22.
limits: The 4 multi-turn tasks that complete the 16 were not rebuilt (only partial values in figures). So 20.9 cannot be reconstructed from the text; it is probably a 16-task mean in absolute points, but this is a guess. Treat as unconfirmed.
agent_relevance: Quote CASCADE as +18.35 points on the 12-task table with a range 2 to 51. Most of the headline comes from a few tasks where zero-shot is near zero.

source: Guo et al. (2026) CASCADE supplementary: human-involved revision (always retain ground-truth case) and discovery steps
finding: Gaps 7 and 3 partial. Retaining the ground-truth case every step improved most tasks but hurt MIMIC-MR, MIMIC-MSR, CMDL and LFD, because the retriever could not manage the growing, diverse bank in limited steps. In a separate test, spending a 10 percent budget of ground-truth labels where no relevant case exists (discovery) beat random placement of the same budget.
numbers: Discovery relative gain over standard CASCADE: Exploit trigger 8.83 percent, UCB trigger 8.73 percent, Random 5.61 percent. Trigger fires when the selected metric falls below the 10th percentile of a 16-long FIFO queue.
limits: Tasks and seeds for the discovery figure are not given in the text read. This is not an LLM novelty gate on self-generated answers; labels come from ground truth.
agent_relevance: A cheap analog of a novelty gate: write when the best existing case has low learned utility. A bank bigger than the retriever can rank can hurt; this is a retrieval-capacity limit, not a reason to refuse a correct case.

source: Zhao, Huang, Xu, Lin, Liu, Huang (2024) ExpeL arXiv 2308.10144, Table 3 and Figure 6
finding: Gap 10: ExpeL has the random-example control. Retrieving the most task-similar successful trajectories beats random successful trajectories by a lot, so relevance of examples, not just count, drives the gain. Experience gathered with retries (success and failure pairs) beat ReAct-only experience.
numbers: ALFWorld SR: ReAct 40.0; random sampled successful trajectories 42.5; reasoning-similarity retrieval 48.5; task-similarity retrieval (ExpeL) 59.0 (order read from table text; labels lost in extraction). HotpotQA insight ablation: ReAct 28.0; hand-crafted insights 32.0; insights with reflections 29.0; gpt-3.5 insights 32.0; ExpeL 39.0 (same caveat).
limits: Cell to label mapping rests on row order. GPT-3.5/4 era models. The random control is on example selection, not on write policy.
agent_relevance: Random same-task examples give about +2.5 points, retrieval relevance about +19. So the retention gain is mostly about having the right case retrievable, not any few-shot examples.

source: Ouyang et al. (2026) ReasoningBank arXiv 2509.25140: judge calibration, Figure 8
finding: Gap 2 evidence for distilled memory. The measured judge (Gemini-2.5-flash) accuracy on WebArena-Shopping was 72.7 percent. Simulated judge accuracy from 100 down to 50 percent moves success only a few points, and every level stays above no memory.
numbers: WebArena-Shopping no-memory 39.0; ReasoningBank 49.7 (Table 1). Figure 8 values across 100/90/80/70/60/50 percent accuracy range from about 47.0 to 52.4 (exact level mapping is not recoverable from PDF text). Success-only 46.5 vs with failures 49.7 (Fig 7). Synapse 40.6 to 41.7, AWM 44.4 to 42.2 when failures are added.
limits: One subset (Shopping, 187 tasks), one judge, one run per level, simulated flips independent of task. At 50 percent accuracy the labels are random, yet the bank still gains: the gain seems to come mostly from distilled strategy text, not from correct labelling. The figure may use test-time scaling, so the baseline match is unclear.
agent_relevance: Distilled strategy stores look insensitive to write-gate noise. A raw-trace store is not (Xiong). So gate quality matters most when we store raw traces.

source: Xiong et al. (2025) arXiv 2505.16067 Table 1: break-even of coarse judges vs fixed seed memory (computed here from the table)
finding: Gap 2 answer for raw-trace storage, by direct comparison of Table 1. Of 12 coarse-judge cells (C1 to C3, four agents), 6 beat the fixed seed memory and 6 do not. Strict (oracle) beats fixed in all 4. Add-all is below fixed in all 4.
numbers: Fixed / add-all / C1 / C2 / C3 / strict. RegAgent 67.53 / 55.48 / 63.18 / 65.78 / 67.35 / 70.95. EHRAgent 16.75 / 13.05 / 26.19 / 32.21 / 34.66 / 38.50. AgentDriver 40.11 / 32.32 / 36.92 / 40.01 / 47.37 / 51.00. CIC-IoT 71.50 / 59.90 / 74.00 / 68.80 / 79.50 / 85.40. Coarse above fixed: EHRAgent x3, AgentDriver C3, CIC-IoT C1 and C3. Memory sizes: fixed 50 to 180 records vs 900 to 3500 for gated runs.
limits: Judge accuracy for C1 to C3 is not given as one percentage, only through evaluator error thresholds (RegAgent 1.6, 1.4, 1.2) and model choice, so a break-even accuracy in percent cannot be read off. C3 is a model fine-tuned on only 300 labelled trajectories. Bank sizes differ, so this is not equal-bank-size.
agent_relevance: Rough rule: a prompted judge is a coin flip against a fixed seed bank; a judge tuned on a few hundred labels usually clears it; only an exact check clearly wins. Prefer code or answer checks over self-judgement when raw traces are stored.

source: Xiong et al. (2025) Section 5: distribution shift and capped memory
finding: Gap 4 partial. Under a task-distribution shift, memory with strict addition and combined deletion stays close to the no-shift runs; in AgentDriver strict addition alone beats the no-shift variant. On EHRAgent, history-based (later-use utility) deletion alone does worse than combined, and periodic deletion helps stabilise. With capacity capped at the initial size (100 EHRAgent, 180 AgentDriver), managed memory still beats the fixed bank.
numbers: Cap sizes 100 and 180 records. Periodic deletion every 500 steps; history-based threshold 0.5 on RegAgent-style setups. Strict-evaluator history deletion on AgentDriver can beat the error-free memory baseline. With a coarse C1 evaluator, history-based deletion lowered AgentDriver and CIC-IoT results in the table text (rows hard to align after extraction, so exact values are not quoted).
limits: Shift is built by reordering test inputs; streams are a few thousand tasks at most; results come from figures and one run.
agent_relevance: Capped deletion by later-use utility is safe only with a reliable utility check; with a noisy judge, add a periodic age-based sweep. Decay over 1000+ tasks is still untested.

source: Liu et al. (2026) SEDM arXiv 2509.09498: verifiable write admission by paired replay
finding: Gaps 1 and 7. Admit a memory only if an A/B replay with and without it improves reward net of token cost. This keeps noisy items out at lower token cost. Separately, in a controlled study memory turns 73 failures into successes but also 32 successes into failures, so a stored, relevant memory does not guarantee benefit at use time.
numbers: FEVER accuracy: no memory 57; G-Memory 62 (3.62M prompt tokens); plus paired-test admission 64 (2.19M tokens, 40 percent fewer); plus self-scheduling 66. HotpotQA EM: 34; 38; 37; 39. Controlled HotpotQA: always-use memory raises success 0.249 to 0.333; a perfect gate would reach 0.399; the learned gate CMG at lambda 0 gets 0.329 with 18 percent fewer input tokens, and at lambda 0.05 keeps 79 percent of the gain with 33 percent fewer tokens.
limits: The admission arm is not isolated from retrieval changes (compared with G-Memory). Small test sets (193 questions in the LoCoMo gate study). The use-time gate is a trained Qwen3-4B, not a free prompt-only signal.
agent_relevance: Best cheap signal found for gap 7: replay the new task with and without the candidate case and keep it only if the outcome improves. It needs a re-run, so use it on a sample or for ambiguous cases.

source: ReMe authors (2025) ReMe arXiv 2512.10696 Table 3: addition rule, failure reflection, utility deletion
finding: Gaps 1, 5, 8. On BFCL-V3 with Qwen3-8B, selective addition (success only) beats full addition by 3.50 points Avg@4 and 2.66 Pass@4. Failure-aware reflection adds about 0.7 more Avg@4, and utility-based deletion adds more Pass@4.
numbers: Rows read in order: full addition, no reflection, no deletion 40.83 Avg@4 / 62.00 Pass@4; selective addition 44.33 / 64.66; plus failure-aware reflection 45.00 / 64.66; plus utility deletion 45.17 / 68.00. No-memory baseline for Qwen3-8B on BFCL-V3 is 24.41 / 28.50 (Table 4). Deletion rule: remove an experience once retrieved at least a threshold number of times if mean contribution u/f is below a threshold.
limits: Checkmark columns were lost in text extraction, so mapping of numbers to ablation rows rests on row order and the text sentence on +3.50 and +2.66. One model, one benchmark.
agent_relevance: Supports: success-only beats add-all; failure lessons add a small amount; later-use-utility deletion works with embedding retrieval. Not equal-token controlled.

source: Zhang et al. (2026) MemRL arXiv 2601.03192: learned utility of stored cases
finding: Gaps 8 and 5. Storing a Q-value per case and updating it from outcomes after each reuse (embedding retrieval, then re-rank by Q) predicts which cases help. About 12 percent of high-Q memories are failure reflections that still help (near misses).
numbers: Learned Q vs observed success rate: Pearson r 0.861; success rate 21.5 percent in the lowest Q bin to 88.1 percent in the highest. Table 1 last-epoch success average: no memory 0.631, RAG 0.679, Mem0 0.681, MemP 0.736, MemRL 0.772 (BigCodeBench 0.595, OS 0.788, DB 0.960, ALFWorld 0.949, HLE 0.570). Retrieval size is an inverted U, best at k1=5, k2=3.
limits: Reward is reused over 10 epochs on the same task set, so last-epoch numbers mix memorisation and learning. On HLE, with low internal similarity (0.186), the gain over the single-task baseline is near zero (0.610 vs 0.606).
agent_relevance: Later-use utility is a workable deletion and ranking signal with ordinary embedding retrieval; no clean coverage sets are needed. Gains vanish when tasks are dissimilar.

source: Sarukkai et al. (2025) Self-generated in-context examples, arXiv 2505.00234: database-level and exemplar-level curation
finding: Gaps 7, 8, 1. Success-only growth (Traj-Bootstrap) beats a fixed human-written bank, and curating by later-use utility Q(trajectory), the outcome-weighted success of tasks where it was retrieved, adds more. Some trajectories marked successful lead to failures when retrieved, because they succeeded despite bad decisions.
numbers: Success rate (ALFWorld / InterCode-SQL / Wordcraft): Fixed-DB 0.73 / 0.75 / 0.55; Traj-Bootstrap 0.89 / 0.79 / 0.64; +DB-curation 0.91 / 0.78 / 0.64; +Exemplar-curation 0.90 / 0.81 / 0.72; both 0.93 / 0.82 / 0.69 (label order follows the table text). Five seeds; 800 training tasks. Best vs worst exemplar selection by Q: the best curve is higher at all database sizes for ALFWorld and Wordcraft.
limits: Labels come from the environment, not a self-judge. Fixed-DB has 10 human examples, so counts differ (no equal-count random control). Curation is noisy early because of low retrieval counts.
agent_relevance: Strongest direct evidence that a retained success must earn its place by later use. Cheap signal: track how often a case is retrieved and the outcomes of those tasks; drop cases with high retrieval and low success.

source: Evo-Memory arXiv 2511.20857 (v2 May 2026): unfiltered failures and task similarity
finding: Gaps 5 and 1. When both successes and failures are stored without filtering, baseline memory methods degrade; ReMem (which can prune and refine) stays robust. Gain correlates with within-dataset task similarity.
numbers: ExpRAG success, default store (Table 1/4) vs with failures stored (Table 3): Gemini 2.5 Flash ALFWorld 0.59 to 0.25; Claude 3.7 Sonnet ScienceWorld 0.46 to 0.27, ALFWorld 0.74 to 0.76. ReMem: Gemini ALFWorld 0.66 to 0.57; Claude ALFWorld 0.92 to 0.92, ScienceWorld 0.62 to 0.69. Task-similarity correlation of ReMem gain: r 0.717 (Gemini) and 0.563 (Claude).
limits: Table 3 text extraction is garbled, so column assignment is by row order. Whether the default store holds successes only is not stated in the text read. Not token controlled; effects are mixed across model and environment.
agent_relevance: Raw failed episodes in a flat similarity store can hurt; a pruning or refinement step is needed if failures are stored.

source: Zheng et al. (2025) LifelongAgentBench arXiv 2505.11942: replay size and backbone strength
finding: Gaps 10 and 1. Past successful trajectories help weak models a lot and strong models little or negatively; more examples can degrade results through length and noise.
numbers: DB: Llama-3.1-8B 0.19 with no experience to 0.78 at 64 examples; Llama-3.1-70B 0.81 to 0.90 at 64. OS: 0.43 to 0.50 at 4 to 16 examples. KG: 0.28 to 0.35 with 1 example. Qwen2.5-32B scores 0.82 without replay with no clear gain. Group self-consistency on DB Llama-8B at 16 examples: 0.61 ungrouped (17874 tokens) vs 0.75 with 16 groups (2888 tokens).
limits: Retrieval pulls recent successful trajectories, so success-only is built in; no failure or novelty arm.
agent_relevance: For a strong model, more retained cases may be pure cost. Expect most memory gain where the model alone is weak.

source: Zhang et al. (2025) ACE arXiv 2510.04618: context collapse and incremental delta updates
finding: Independent corroboration of the rewriting harm. A monolithic LLM rewrite of an accumulated playbook collapsed 18,282 tokens to 122 in one step and dropped accuracy below the no-adaptation baseline. ACE avoids it by appending delta bullets with dedup. Without ground-truth or execution signals ACE and Dynamic Cheatsheet can degrade.
numbers: AppWorld case: step 60 context 18,282 tokens, accuracy 66.7; next step 122 tokens, accuracy 57.1; baseline 63.7. Ablation without incremental updates: test-normal TGC 67.3 vs 76.2 with them. Harmful reflector every X steps on FiNER: X=5 gives 76.1 (+5.4 over base), no noise 78.3 (+7.6). ACE average +10.6 percent on agents, +8.6 percent on finance.
limits: ACE is itself a consolidation method that gains, so the lesson is about how to update (append, merge), not whether to distil. One collapse case study, shown on Dynamic Cheatsheet.
agent_relevance: Use delta appends with dedup for any lesson store; never regenerate the whole store. Moderate self-judged noise is tolerated in an appended playbook.

source: Gap-search status: Yang and Zhu coverage efficiency for LLM agents (no direct replication found)
finding: Gap 3 stays open. No LLM-agent paper in the sources read tests a store-only-if-no-stored-case-solves-it gate against add-success at equal bank size. Nearest items: CASCADE discovery trigger (d07), SEDM paired-test admission (d12), Sarukkai curation (d15).
numbers: No saturation bank size was measured. Sarukkai curves run to 800 training tasks and still rise for ALFWorld; Memento showed no inflexion over 5 passes (earlier file).
limits: The web search quota was used up during this gap search and the arXiv and OpenAlex APIs were rate-limited, so the scan was limited to papers already known by id. A missing replication is not proof of absence.
agent_relevance: Run it ourselves: a novelty-gated store vs add-success on a small stream is a cheap, new experiment.

source: Gap-search status: equal-token write gate comparison (add-all vs success-only vs novelty vs success plus lessons)
finding: Gap 1 stays open. Pairwise pieces exist: add-all vs success-only (Xiong, ReMe), success-only vs success plus lessons (ReasoningBank, ReMe), curated vs success-only (Sarukkai). None runs all four arms with fixed retrieval and equal token budget on a reasoning task.
numbers: Gains over add-all: ReMe +3.50 Avg@4 for selective addition; Xiong 3.7 to 12.1 points. Gains from failure lessons: ReMe +0.7 Avg@4, ReasoningBank +3.2 on Shopping. Different models, tasks and token costs.
limits: Aggregation across papers mixes backbones and metrics; the ordering is suggestive only.
agent_relevance: Rank by current evidence: curated or utility-pruned success store >= success-only > add-all raw traces; failure lessons a small plus; novelty untested.
